content.title: About
content.content: A multiple meat sandwich (or sub) is a popular restaurant offering consisting of a long roll split lengthwise and filled with a variety of cooked meats such as ham, roast beef, chicken, salami, and sometimes bacon. It is often topped with cheese, fresh vegetables, sauces, and spices. The sandwich can be served cold or lightly warmed and makes a hearty meal for lunch or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first versions appeared in the United States in the early 1920s and quickly became a signature item of many delicatessens.
These subs are often called “hero” sandwiches because of their large protein and calorie content.
Some restaurants use more than five types of meat, including smoked turkey and pastrami.
Traditional sauces include mustard or mayonnaise, sometimes blended with herbs.
The multi‑meat version is frequently featured on menus for athletes and people with high energy needs.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: The assortment of meats provides complete amino acids that support muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Red meats like roast beef are rich in heme iron and zinc, which aid immune function and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for nervous system health and energy production.

items.title: Satiety and sustained energy
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates in the roll provides lasting fullness and steady energy levels.

items.title: Benefits from vegetables
items.content: Added lettuce, tomato, and onion contribute vitamin C, fiber, and antioxidants.

items.title: High calories and fat
items.content: The large amount of meat and sauces makes the sandwich calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed meats like salami and ham are often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Meat allergies
items.content: Some individuals may react to specific meats or additives such as nitrites.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient reheating can lead to bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically cut in half and eaten by hand. It can be warmed in an oven or on a grill to melt the cheese and lightly toast the roll. Common sides include fries, a side salad, or pickles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, keep the meats separate and the roll in a dry place to prevent sogginess.
